newsitem.title: BOSNIA: UN condemns new eviction wave in Mostar.
newsitem.headline: UN condemns new eviction wave in Mostar.

text.p: U.N. officials on Wednesday called the eviction from west Mostar of an elderly handicapped Moslem woman who later died an act of "barbarity" and accused Croat thugs of trying to purge their territory of minorities.

An autopsy showed that Rukija Bejtovic, 71, died of heart failure after she was thrown out of her apartment during the Christmas holiday, said Alex Ivanko, spokesman for United Nations police monitors.
Bejtovic went missing on Christmas Day and her body was found this week in an abandoned building outside Mostar, the largest city in southern Bosnia.
"We believe this is an act of barbarity and words fail us," Ivanko told reporters.
A Croat soldier who moved into the apartment was detained by the Bosnian Croat militia but released after 72 hours as local police decided not to press charges, Ivanko said.
The eviction was the latest example of a systematic purge of non-Croats from the western sector of Mostar over the past three months, Ivanko and U.N. human rights workers said.
A 1993-94 war between Bosnian Croats and Moslems split the town into Croat and Moslem sectors and human rights workers say gangsters dominate the Croat-held western side.

Peter Fitzgerald, commissioner of the U.N.-affiliated International Police Task Force (IPTF) in postwar Bosnia, was extremely concerned that Bejtovic died while a crime was being carried out, Ivanko said.
Bosnian Croat police were also failing to cooperate with the 100 IPTF monitors stationed in Mostar, refusing to provide police reports or answer queries from the monitors, he said.
Moslem and Croat police units now conduct some joint patrols in Mostar but Ivanko said the city's police forces operated separately in reality.
"The unified police force is not very effective. It's the police forces in west and east Mostar who are running the show," Ivanko said.
IPTF planned to exert "political pressure" to force Croat authorities to halt the expulsions, he said. But similar protests in the past have proved fruitless.
Only some 3,000 Moslems and 800 Serbs still live in western Mostar, said Kris Janowski, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees in the Bosnian capital Sarajevo.
Croat authorities appear intent on pushing out the remaining minorities and selling off their property, he said.
A shortage of housing, rampant lawlessness and ethnic hatred make for a "very grim picture" in Mostar, he said.
More than two years of European Union administration, including 270 million German marks ($180 million) in reconstruction aid, have failed to reunify Mostar.
The EU's mandate expired on December 31, 1996.
Janowski said a climate of fear and intimidation discouraged ordinary people from crossing the bridges that span the Neretva river separating Moslem and Croat sectors.

"What has happened is that bridges have been physically built across the river, but they remain physical bridges, whereas in terms of reintegration the city is essentially as divided as ever," Janowski said.
